title: Algorithmic Design Features
subtitle: Engagement-Based Ranking and the Limits of Reactive Regulation
author: Delaney McLaughlin

hook.t: In November 2017, Molly Russell, a 14-year-old from Harrow, north-west London, died from an act of self-harm while suffering from depression and the negative effects of online content, after months of viewing self-harm and suicide content on Instagram and Pinterest.
During her inquest, it was revealed that of the 16,300 posts Molly saved, shared or liked on Instagram in the six months before her death, 2,100 were related to depression, self-harm or suicide.
Pinterest went as far as emailing her recommendations with subject lines such as "10 depression pins you might like."

These posts did not reach Molly by chance. The Children's Commissioner for England said the platforms' algorithms, "designed to maximise users' attention and engagement," recommended "an increasing volume of harrowing content to Molly," and the coroner found that the platforms' algorithms produced, in some circumstances, "binge periods of images, video-clips and text," some of it "selected and provided without Molly requesting them."

Molly's case is not isolated. The U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 advisory reports that up to 95% of youth aged 13 to 17 say they use a social media platform. It also cites a study of U.S. adolescents aged 12 to 15 in which those who spent more than three hours a day on social media faced double the risk of poor mental health outcomes, including symptoms of depression and anxiety. As of 2021, 8th and 10th graders spent an average of 3.5 hours a day on social media.

thesis.t: Governments around the world have increasingly responded to the harms that social media poses to young users through age-based bans and access restrictions, which determine who is able to use these platforms but do not address the engagement-driven design that causes the harm in the first place. This reflects a broader pattern of reactive correction rather than proactive regulation of the platforms' structural design. Explainable AI methods such as LIME, SHAP, and counterfactual explanations offer a way for regulators to examine how these ranking systems operate before harm occurs, although applying them in practice presents significant challenges that current policy has yet to account for.

philosophy.q: Why is engagement-based ranking ethically wrong when it reaches vulnerable users?

intro.t: The harms produced by engagement-based ranking cannot be understood solely as technical failures, as they reflect value choices embedded in how these systems are designed and what they are built to prioritize. The four principles of biomedical ethics (respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice), set out by Beauchamp and Childress, provide a framework for evaluating these choices and identifying where they fall short.

body.t: Engagement-based ranking is built to predict which content a user is most likely to engage with and to keep supplying it, which can undermine the conditions that make voluntary choice possible, particularly for adolescents, whose capacity for impulse control and self-regulation is still developing. This builds on the argument, developed in earlier work on AI companions, that autonomy is not merely a choice but the set of conditions that make choice possible.

These systems are built to predict and reward engagement, and the Surgeon General's advisory notes that social media platforms are often designed to maximize user engagement. On this essay's reading, any good the user receives is therefore incidental to the system's engagement objective. Meta itself describes its ranking as predicting how valuable a piece of content might be to a user so it can be shown sooner, combining a wide variety of predictions, some based on behavior (such as whether a user is likely to share a post) and some based on user feedback received through surveys.

When platforms are aware that their ranking systems amplify harmful content to vulnerable users and continue to deploy them without meaningful safeguards, the resulting harm is foreseeable and therefore preventable. In Molly Russell's case, the coroner found that the platforms' use of algorithms resulted, "in some circumstances," in "binge periods" of images, video clips and text, some of it "selected and provided without Molly requesting them," and that the material she viewed contributed to her death "in a more than minimal way." The Children's Commissioner went further, saying the algorithms, "designed to maximise users' attention and engagement," recommended "an increasing volume of harrowing content" to her.

The consequences of engagement-driven design do not fall evenly, as they are concentrated on those least able to protect themselves, including minors, users experiencing psychological distress, and populations in regions with limited regulatory oversight. In Myanmar, Facebook's engagement-based algorithms operated in a country where it held near-total market dominance by 2017 and had become, for many people, their primary news source, and Amnesty International concluded that Meta "substantially contributed" to the atrocities against the Rohingya.

takeaway.t: Engagement is not a neutral metric, and the decision to optimize for it is an ethical choice that platforms are responsible for.

policy.q: Why do current laws fail to address engagement-based ranking, and what would need to change?

intro.t: Current legislation addressing youth and social media can be grouped into four categories: access-based measures that restrict who can use platforms, design-based measures that regulate how platforms are built, transparency-based measures that require platforms to disclose or explain how their systems operate, and liability, where courts assign responsibility after harm has occurred. Much of the most prominent recent legislative activity has focused on access, while design and transparency measures remain limited, recent, and largely untested. Each profile below records what a measure targets, what it requires engineers and designers to build, whether it requires any form of explanation, which explainable AI methods could provide evidence of compliance, how feasible it is to implement, and what it leaves untouched.

targets.t: Account access for users under 16 on platforms including Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, X, YouTube, Kick, and Twitch; standalone messaging, online gaming, and most health and education services are not covered.

build.t: Platforms must take reasonable steps to keep under-16s off their services and cannot rely on users self-reporting their age alone, with fines of up to AUD 49.5 million.

xai.t: None. The law does not require platforms to explain or alter how content is ranked.

xai_methods.t: Not applicable. Compliance is demonstrated through age assurance accuracy rather than through explanations of the ranking system.

feasibility.t: Moderate to low. Age assurance raises accuracy and privacy concerns, and only early outcome data have been reported. eSafety's three-month evaluation (July 2026) found that the share of 10-to-15-year-olds holding an age-restricted account fell from 52.4% to 42.1%. Many children kept their accounts, most often because the platform had not yet asked them to confirm their age or had estimated it incorrectly. Most children reported little to no change in their wellbeing. eSafety says it is too early to tell whether the ban's intended outcomes will be achieved.

gap.t: The ban itself does nothing to the ranking system that users 16 and over encounter; any changes, such as Instagram's Teen Accounts for 16- and 17-year-olds, are voluntary platform choices rather than requirements of the law.

measures.juris: Denmark, France, Greece, Spain, Slovenia, Indonesia, Malaysia, UK
measures.name: Planned or proposed age bans

status.t: Status as of Oct. 18, 2026: Malaysia (under 16) in force since June 1, 2026, with age checks for existing users phased in over up to six months; Indonesia (under 16) restricting major high-risk platforms, with under-16 accounts deactivated in phases from March 28, 2026; Denmark (under 15) draft bill issued in September 2026, to go to Parliament in early 2027 with a target start of July 1, 2027; France (under 15) passed Parliament on July 21, but the Constitutional Council struck the ban down on Aug. 14; Greece (under 15) bill before Parliament, final vote scheduled for Oct. 22, starting Jan. 1, 2027 if passed; Spain (under 16) bill still in Congress and could stall now that Parliament is dissolved before the Nov. 29 snap election; the UK announced on June 15 that it will ban under-16s, with the first regulations due by the end of 2026 and the ban expected in early to spring 2027.

targets.t: Account access by age. Greece cites anxiety, sleep problems, and addictive platform design as its reasons, yet its proposed under-15 ban regulates access, through an age limit and age verification, rather than the design itself.

build.t: Age assurance systems, in several cases modeled on Australia's approach.

feasibility.t: Uncertain. Critics including Amnesty Tech argue that such bans are ineffective and out of step with how young people live online, and there are concerns about privacy and invasive age verification.

gap.t: These measures identify addictive design as the problem while regulating only who may be exposed to it.

status.t: Final rules released in July 2026 (July 28); the law takes effect January 25, 2027.

targets.t: Algorithmically personalized "addictive feeds", and notifications about those feeds between midnight and 6 a.m. Eastern, for New York users under 18 (in practice, any user the platform has not confirmed as an adult through age assurance), unless a parent gives verifiable consent; applies to platforms where at least 20% of monthly active users' time is spent on such feeds, with an exemption for smaller platforms.

build.t: Age assurance with at least one option other than government ID, certified (tested) annually with results retained for 10 years; a default feed for minors limited to accounts they follow or select, in a set sequence such as chronological order, instead of the algorithmically personalized feed; data minimization and deletion for age and consent data.

xai.t: None. The law restricts personalization but does not require the platform to explain how the personalized feed ranks content.

xai_methods.t: Compliance could be evidenced by showing that minors' feeds receive no personalized ranking signals; SHAP or permutation importance on a minor's feed would show zero contribution from user-history features.

feasibility.t: Moderate. Turning personalization off is technically simple, while age assurance is the harder and more contested component.

gap.t: Once a parent consents, the engagement-optimized feed returns unchanged, and the law does not address what the ranking system optimizes for.

measures.name: Protecting Our Kids from Social Media Addiction Act (SB 976)

status.t: Partly in effect. On September 9, 2025, the Ninth Circuit refused to block the addictive-feed and private-by-default provisions at the preliminary-injunction stage, so they can be enforced. It also held that the limit on showing like counts is likely unconstitutional. Litigation continues. In August 2026 a federal judge again refused to block the feed provisions, this time in new suits by Meta, TikTok and YouTube, and those companies are appealing. The age-assurance requirements begin January 1, 2027.

targets.t: Addictive feeds, defined as feeds where user-generated or user-shared content is recommended, selected, or prioritized based on information provided by or associated with the user, offered to minors without verifiable parental consent; private-by-default accounts.

build.t: A non-personalized feed path for minors, parental consent flows, and privacy-protective account defaults.

xai_methods.t: As with New York, attribution methods could verify that user-history signals are absent from minors' rankings.

feasibility.t: Contested in court; in September 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that the default barring minors' accounts from showing like counts was likely unconstitutional (a content-based rule that fails strict scrutiny) and ordered it enjoined, while letting the private-by-default setting and, for now, the addictive-feed limits stand. This suggests the legal limit falls on content-based design rules rather than on regulating interface design as such.

gap.t: Defines the harm by whether a feed is personalized, not by what the feed is optimized to maximize.

measures.name: Online Safety Act, Protection of Children Codes (Ofcom)

status.t: Children's safety duties and Ofcom's Protection of Children Codes in force since July 25, 2025.

targets.t: Under Ofcom's Protection of Children Code (in force 25 July 2025), services likely to be accessed by children that run a content recommender system and are assessed as medium or high risk for certain harmful content are recommended to design their feeds so that such content is kept out of children's feeds or given low prominence. Primary priority content (e.g., pornography, suicide and self-harm material) should be excluded outright. Other priority and identified non-designated content may be excluded or demoted. The Act requires a children's risk assessment and a duty to keep it up to date, and Ofcom recommends reviewing it at least annually.

build.t: Recommender systems set up to filter the most harmful content out of children's feeds and reduce the prominence of other harmful content (Ofcom does not require classifiers or any specific technology), a children's risk assessment kept up to date (Ofcom recommends reviewing it at least annually), highly effective age assurance on services that allow priority harmful content, including higher-risk services with recommender feeds, and tools for reporting and complaints.

xai.t: Indirect. The codes do not require explanations, but demonstrating that harmful content receives low prominence requires evidence about how the recommender ranks it.

xai_methods.t: SHAP and counterfactuals could test whether a harmful-content flag actually lowers a post's rank, and deletion tests could check that the demotion is real rather than nominal.

feasibility.t: The most direct design rule of any jurisdiction reviewed, but it depends on classifiers correctly identifying harmful content, which the companion chatbot cases show can fail when context and phrasing matter.

gap.t: Targets categories of content rather than the engagement objective, so content that falls outside the listed categories but still harms a vulnerable user continues to be amplified.

measures.name: Digital Services Act: recommender transparency (Art. 27) and non-profiling option (Art. 38)

status.t: In force: the Digital Services Act has applied to online platforms since 17 February 2024 (micro and small enterprises are exempt from Article 27). Article 38 applies to very large online platforms and very large online search engines, with obligations starting four months after the Commission designates them.

targets.t: Online platforms that use recommender systems must set out in their terms and conditions, in plain and intelligible language, the main parameters of their recommender systems, including the criteria most significant in determining the information suggested and the reasons for the relative importance of those parameters; very large online platforms must also offer at least one option for each recommender system that is not based on profiling.

build.t: Plain-language documentation of ranking criteria, user controls, and a non-profiling feed that functions as a genuine alternative.

xai.t: Yes, but only at the level of the system as a whole: because the "main parameters" must be set out in the terms and conditions, the requirement works as a global explanation requirement (our reading; the DSA does not use that term). However, the requirement can be interpreted in multiple ways, and commentators report that the first round of DSA audits showed variation in how platforms defined it.

xai_methods.t: Global methods such as permutation feature importance or mean SHAP values are the natural technical basis for a "main parameters" disclosure, and the five evaluation tests could become the standard for whether that disclosure is adequate.

feasibility.t: Feasible, but Article 27's disclosure requirements can be read in multiple ways, and without consistent disclosures it is hard to compare how recommender systems are optimized across platforms; the Knight-Georgetown Institute's Better Feeds guidelines call for platforms to disclose specific input data and weights.

gap.t: A disclosure that is accurate but vague satisfies the law while telling a regulator or a user very little.

measures.name: DSA systemic risk assessments, independent audits, and researcher data access (Arts. 34, 35, 37, 40)

status.t: The Commission adopted the delegated act on researcher data access on 1 July 2025 and published it on 2 July 2025. It appeared in the Official Journal as Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2050 and entered into force on 29 October 2025, when vetted researchers could start requesting platform data. Vetting is slower than the Commission's "as of October" target: in May 2026 national Digital Services Coordinators were still assessing the first 49 applications.

targets.t: Very large platforms must assess and mitigate systemic risks, undergo independent audits, and give vetted researchers access to internal data for studying systemic risks in the EU.

build.t: Risk assessment processes, audit-ready evidence, and secure data access pipelines for vetted researchers.

xai.t: Implicit. Researchers with internal data access are the only outside party who could actually run LIME, SHAP, or counterfactual analyses on a real ranking system.

xai_methods.t: This is the provision that makes every other XAI method possible, since attribution methods require access to the model or at least to its inputs and outputs.

feasibility.t: Promising but still being put into practice; a 2025 Knight-Georgetown Institute analysis says platforms have given inconsistent access to publicly available data, and calls for validated, consistent metrics of harm, particularly for at-risk populations.

gap.t: Access is limited to research on systemic risks in the EU; outside the EU no equivalent mechanism is yet operating (the UK's Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 lets the government create one, and US proposals such as the Platform Accountability and Transparency Act have not passed).

measures.name: DSA guidelines on the protection of minors (Art. 28)

status.t: Adopted by the European Commission in July 2025 (adopted 2 July, presented 14 July, published in the Official Journal 10 October 2025).

targets.t: Under the European Commission's 2025 guidelines on protecting minors under the DSA, minors should be able to reset their recommended feeds completely and permanently, get a meaningful explanation of why each piece of content was recommended, and modify or influence how their recommender systems work. Platforms should not expose minors to persuasive design aimed mainly at engagement, such as indefinite scrolling and virtual rewards for repeated actions, and features such as streaks should be off by default.

build.t: Child-facing explanation features, feed reset controls, private and secure defaults, and the removal of overuse features.

xai.t: Yes, at the level of the individual: this is a local explanation requirement written for a child as the audience.

xai_methods.t: Local methods (LIME, SHAP) supply the raw reasons, and counterfactuals are the closest to something a child could act on, but none of the three was designed with a child as the intended audience.

feasibility.t: The most demanding explanation requirement reviewed. The technical lens of this project shows how far current methods are from producing an explanation a 14-year-old could understand and use.

gap.t: The guidelines say what a child should understand without specifying how an explanation would be tested for whether a child actually understands it.

status.t: Prohibitions have applied since February 2, 2025, with national enforcement powers from August 2, 2025 and fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

targets.t: AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities linked to age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting a person's behaviour in a manner that causes, or is reasonably likely to cause, significant harm (AI Act, Art. 5(1)(b)).

build.t: Evidence that a system does not exploit age-related vulnerabilities; in practice this would require testing recommender behavior on minors specifically.

xai.t: Implicit. Proving or disproving exploitation would require showing why a system behaves differently for vulnerable users.

xai_methods.t: Counterfactual analysis (does the feed change when only the user's age-related signals change?) and attribution methods on minors' feeds could provide this evidence.

feasibility.t: Untested. Whether engagement-based ranking qualifies as exploiting age-related vulnerabilities has not yet been decided, and the significant-harm threshold sets a high bar.

gap.t: The strongest design-based language in any jurisdiction reviewed, but it has not yet been applied to social media ranking.

status.t: Approved by the Senate Commerce Committee by voice vote on August 5, 2026 and awaiting a full Senate vote; a prior version passed the Senate 91-3 in July 2024 but stalled in the House.

targets.t: A duty of care requiring platforms to exercise reasonable care in the design of their features to prevent and mitigate specified harms to minors (such as eating disorders, suicidal behaviors and compulsive usage), limits on addictive design features by default, and protective default settings for minors.

build.t: Protective defaults and design changes to features identified as addictive; specifics would depend on the final text and enforcement guidance.

xai_methods.t: A duty of care would create demand for evidence of foreseeable harm, which attribution methods and outcome audits could provide.

feasibility.t: Pending. A duty of care is flexible but leaves the standard of evidence to be determined after the fact.

gap.t: Not yet law. The Senate Commerce Committee approved it on August 5, 2026, Sen. Rand Paul blocked a unanimous-consent passage attempt on September 30, 2026, and the House passed a different bill (the KIDS Act, H.R. 7757, 267-117) without KOSA's duty of care.

status.t: In March 2026, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent; it awarded $3 million in compensatory damages and recommended a further $3 million in punitive damages. Meta filed a notice of appeal in July 2026, and YouTube filed its own less than a week later.

targets.t: Design features such as infinite scroll, endless feeds, and autoplay, which plaintiffs targeted to sidestep Section 230 protections for third-party content.

build.t: Nothing yet; a verdict assigns responsibility for past harm rather than setting forward-looking engineering requirements.

xai_methods.t: In litigation, attribution analyses of internal ranking data could show whether design features rather than content drove a plaintiff's exposure.

feasibility.t: Courts can assign responsibility only after harm has already occurred, one case at a time.

gap.t: Liability is the clearest recognition yet that design causes harm, and the clearest example of reactive correction.

status.t: On March 24, 2026, a New Mexico jury found that Meta violated the state's Unfair Practices Act and imposed a $375 million civil penalty (75,000 violations at the $5,000 statutory maximum). On August 6, 2026, after a separate bench trial, the judge found that Meta's platforms created a public nuisance and ordered Meta to pay a further $567 million into an abatement fund, bringing the total to about $942 million. Meta has asked the court to amend the judgment or grant a new trial, and says it will appeal.

targets.t: Among the practices at issue were the role of Meta's algorithms in prioritizing sensational or harmful content, allegedly addictive features, and statements about platform safety, which the jury found false or misleading.

build.t: After a May 2026 bench trial on the state's public nuisance claim, the court in August 2026 ordered Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund on top of the jury's penalty, but declined to order changes to features such as infinite scroll and autoplay, saying those "require legislative or executive branch action"; Meta says it will appeal.

xai_methods.t: As above, attribution and counterfactual analyses of internal data could have supported or rebutted claims about algorithmic prioritization.

gap.t: Confirms that a jury will hold a platform responsible for what its algorithms prioritize, but only after the harm.

health.t: Healthcare offers a useful comparison. The Coalition for Health AI's (CHAI) voluntary draft guide sets out a six-stage lifecycle in which designing the AI system comes before it is engineered, assessed, piloted, or deployed, and it stresses independent review to uncover risks before deployment. In the United States, social media ranking systems face no comparable general requirement to be evaluated at the design stage, so scrutiny has largely come after harm has occurred, often through litigation. Europe has started to move: the EU's Digital Services Act requires very large platforms to assess systemic risks from their algorithmic systems before deploying high-impact features, and the UK's Online Safety Act requires a new children's risk assessment before any significant change to a service's design or operation.

audit.t: A design-first approach would require platforms to answer the same questions an auditor would ask: what requirement applies, what evidence proves it, who reviewed the evidence, what failed, and what changed because of the finding. An overall accuracy figure, verbal assurances, or informal promises to fix issues later count as weak evidence.

memos.title: Regulate the objective, not only the feature

body.t: Current design laws switch individual features on or off. The simulation in this project shows that removing a single ranking signal does not remove the behavior, because correlated signals take its place. A memo would recommend that regulators examine what a ranking system is optimized to maximize for minors and require outcome measures, such as the share of distress-related content in a minor's top recommendations, rather than feature lists alone.

memos.title: Set a testing standard for explanations

body.t: The DSA requires platforms to set out the main parameters of their recommender systems but does not say how such an explanation should be judged. A memo would propose adopting the five evaluation tests, fidelity, faithfulness, completeness, stability, and human usefulness, as the standard an explanation must meet before it counts as evidence of compliance.

memos.title: Require design-stage review for systems that rank content for minors

body.t: Following the healthcare model, changes to ranking systems that reach minors would undergo documented, independent review before deployment rather than after harm, with audit evidence organized around requirements rather than assurances.

memos.title: Extend independent data access beyond the EU

body.t: Every XAI method depends on access to the model or its data. A memo would examine how researcher and auditor access similar to the DSA's Article 40 could be adopted in the United States, so that outside parties can test ranking systems instead of relying on platform self-reporting.

takeaway.t: Access-based regulation is widespread, while design-based regulation remains rare, recent, and largely unproven, and almost none of it specifies how an explanation of a ranking system should be tested.

technical.q: Can explainable AI show regulators how a ranking system actually works, and how far can those explanations be trusted?

intro.t: Because platforms generally do not make their trained ranking models available for outside inspection, this project uses a simulated feed to demonstrate how explainable AI methods could be applied to engagement-based ranking and where they fall short. A gradient-boosted model was trained on 20,000 simulated post impressions to predict engagement, and then used to rank the feed of one simulated 14-year-old who has recently engaged with distress-related content. Because the data is simulated, the true drivers of engagement are known, which makes it possible to check the explanations against the truth.

what.t: Fits a simple linear model around one prediction by perturbing its inputs and watching how the output changes, producing an approximate reason for a single ranking.

result.t: For the top-ranked post, LIME named the user's past engagement with the topic as the main reason in 39 of 40 reruns, but its simple model reproduced only about 62% of the ranker's local behavior, and it ranked "hours since posted" as the third most important factor, which SHAP did not.

what.t: Divides a prediction among its input features using Shapley values from game theory, so that every feature's contribution plus a baseline adds up exactly to the model's output.

result.t: SHAP named the emotional intensity of the post as the largest contributor, nearly tied with the user's past engagement with the topic, and its contributions summed exactly to the model's score. Across the whole dataset, SHAP's ranking of features closely matched the true drivers of engagement (rank correlation 0.964).

what.t: Describe the smallest meaningful change that would produce a different outcome, which, under Dr. Bent's framing, must be actionable: within the person's control and achievable within the relevant time frame, and never involving attributes the person cannot change.

result.t: No change to the teen's own engagement history alone could remove the top post from her top three; even with no past engagement with the topic at all, it would still rank #2. It only fell out of the top three when the post's emotional intensity was reduced from 0.86 to 0.05, a property of the content and the ranking, not of the user.

proxy.t: Distress-related posts made up 15.7% of all simulated posts but 47.4% of the top 10% of rankings, even though the model was never told which posts were distress-related; it learned to favor them because they produce engagement.

design_cf.t: Retraining the ranker without emotional intensity as a signal lowered the share of distress-related posts in the top 10% from 47.4% to 38.0%, but the same two distress-related posts remained at the top of the teen's feed, because correlated signals such as watch completion and comment rate carried the same information.

tests_intro.t: Dr. Bent's evaluation framework asks that tests match the explanation's intended claim and its audience. Each test below is scored on the simulated demo.

body.t: SHAP passes: its contributions reproduce the model's score exactly. LIME is partial: its local surrogate explained about 62% of the model's behavior around the post.

Removing the two features SHAP ranked highest lowered the post's score by 0.354, compared with an average of 0.066 when two features were removed in random order, indicating that SHAP identified features the model actually uses.

SHAP's top three features accounted for 84.4% of the post's ranking. A platform-style one-line reason (a paraphrase of TikTok's "Why this video" wording), "This video is similar to content you've interacted with," accounts for only 35.1%, leaving 64.9% unexplained, including the post's emotional intensity, its single largest driver.

LIME's top reason held in 39 of 40 reruns and did not change across kernel widths, and SHAP's top three features did not change when the post was altered slightly. Stability has to be tested rather than assumed, because LIME's sampling makes every run slightly different.

Not tested with real users in this project. Judged against the intended audience, a SHAP value in probability units is not something a 14-year-old or a legislator can act on, and the only actionable counterfactual places the burden on the child rather than on the platform.

takeaway.t: Explanations of ranking systems are possible but fragile, and a regulator who accepts an explanation without testing it is accepting weak evidence.

public.q: What do platforms tell users about why they see what they see, and how does that compare with what is actually happening?

intro.t: Platforms already offer users some explanation of their feeds. These features are the point at which explainable AI actually reaches the public, so they are the most direct test of whether explanations serve the people they are meant for.

says.t: Announced in December 2022 for rollout over the following weeks, it gives short reasons such as that a video is similar to content the user has interacted with or searched for, is from an account the user follows, or is popular or was posted recently in the user's region.

limits.t: Popular Science reported that TikTok's "Why this video" feature would not reveal any major details about how the algorithm works and would give users only a hint as to why a video was shown. TikTok itself presented the feature as a step toward "meaningful transparency" and said it would expand it to bring "more granularity and transparency."

features.name: Meta, "Why am I seeing this?" and system cards

says.t: In June 2023, Meta released 22 system cards describing how AI ranks content across Facebook and Instagram, and said it would expand "Why Am I Seeing This?" to Instagram's Reels tab and Explore and to Facebook Reels in the coming weeks, letting users tap an individual reel to see how their previous activity may have informed the models that shape the reels they see.

limits.t: Meta states that there is a limit to what it can disclose safely, including the signals it uses to keep bad content out of Feeds, because disclosing them might make it easier to circumvent its defenses, and it acknowledges that not everyone will find information just because it is published on its website.

says.t: Under the EU Digital Services Act, very large platforms must offer at least one option for each of their recommender systems that is not based on profiling (Art. 38). Users must be able to switch to it at any time from the part of the interface where the feed is ranked (Art. 27(3); Recital 94).

limits.t: Researchers have cited a civil society complaint alleging that Meta is not meaningfully implementing these recommender requirements on Facebook and Instagram. In a separate case brought by Bits of Freedom, a Dutch court found in October 2025 that Meta was not complying with DSA Articles 27(3) and 38, and the Court of Appeal upheld that ruling in March 2026.

gap.t: In the simulation, the reason a platform would most likely show (paraphrasing TikTok's "Why this video" feature), "This video is similar to content you've interacted with," is accurate, but it accounts for only 35.1% of why the top post was ranked first. It does not tell the user that the post's emotional intensity was the largest single factor, and the only change it implies she can make, engaging less with similar content, would not remove the post from the top of her feed.

stakes.t: In March 2026, two juries reached verdicts against Meta within a day of each other: a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent in a case focused on design features such as infinite scroll and autoplay, and a New Mexico jury imposed a $375 million penalty in a case that included algorithms prioritizing sensational or harmful content.

These dynamics are not limited to young users: Amnesty International found that Facebook's engagement-driven news feed, ranking and recommendation algorithms amplified anti-Rohingya hatred in Myanmar in the years before the 2017 atrocities (which the US government has determined to be genocide), and that Meta's later fixes, such as banning military leaders' accounts and adding Burmese-language moderators, focused on content moderation rather than on changing those algorithms.

takeaway.t: The explanations users receive today are true but partial, and they describe the user's own behavior far more than they describe the design choices that shape the feed.

conclusion.t: Taken together, these four lenses show that the harms of engagement-based ranking are foreseeable, that current regulation largely addresses who is exposed rather than how exposure is designed, and that explainable AI can make these systems inspectable only if explanations are tested against standards that match the people relying on them. Every meaningful correction to date has come after someone was harmed, and the tools to look before that point already exist.

limitations.t: The feed, users, and ranking model are simulated. Most real platform ranking systems are not available for outside inspection (X is a partial exception: it has open-sourced its For You ranking code and blend weights, but not its trained models or data), so the demo shows how the methods behave on a system with known properties rather than what any specific platform does.
Human usefulness was assessed against the stated audience rather than tested with real users.
Policy statuses are accurate as of October 2026 and are changing quickly; several measures are under legal challenge or pending.
Several policy summaries rely on reputable secondary sources (law firm analyses and news reporting) rather than the full legal text; these are cited individually in the source ledger.

ledger.text: In November 2017, Molly Russell, a 14-year-old from Harrow, north-west London, died from an act of self-harm while suffering from depression and the negative effects of online content, after months of viewing self-harm and suicide content on Instagram and Pinterest.
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook

ledger.text: During her inquest, it was revealed that of the 16,300 posts Molly saved, shared or liked on Instagram in the six months before her death, 2,100 were related to depression, self-harm or suicide.
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook stat callouts

ledger.text: Pinterest went as far as emailing her recommendations with subject lines such as "10 depression pins you might like."
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook

ledger.text: These posts did not reach Molly by chance. The Children's Commissioner for England said the platforms' algorithms, "designed to maximise users' attention and engagement," recommended "an increasing volume of harrowing content to Molly," and the coroner found that the platforms' algorithms produced, in some circumstances, "binge periods of images, video-clips and text," some of it "selected and provided without Molly requesting them."
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook

ledger.text: Molly's case is not isolated. The U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 advisory reports that up to 95% of youth aged 13 to 17 say they use a social media platform. It also cites a study of U.S. adolescents aged 12 to 15 in which those who spent more than three hours a day on social media faced double the risk of poor mental health outcomes, including symptoms of depression and anxiety. As of 2021, 8th and 10th graders spent an average of 3.5 hours a day on social media.
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook stat callouts

ledger.text: The harms produced by engagement-based ranking cannot be understood solely as technical failures, as they reflect value choices embedded in how these systems are designed and what they are built to prioritize. The four principles of biomedical ethics (respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice), set out by Beauchamp and Childress, provide a framework for evaluating these choices and identifying where they fall short.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens intro

ledger.text: Engagement-based ranking is built to predict which content a user is most likely to engage with and to keep supplying it, which can undermine the conditions that make voluntary choice possible, particularly for adolescents, whose capacity for impulse control and self-regulation is still developing. This builds on the argument, developed in earlier work on AI companions, that autonomy is not merely a choice but the set of conditions that make choice possible.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens, Autonomy; Poster: Philosophical quadrant

ledger.text: These systems are built to predict and reward engagement, and the Surgeon General's advisory notes that social media platforms are often designed to maximize user engagement. On this essay's reading, any good the user receives is therefore incidental to the system's engagement objective. Meta itself describes its ranking as predicting how valuable a piece of content might be to a user so it can be shown sooner, combining a wide variety of predictions, some based on behavior (such as whether a user is likely to share a post) and some based on user feedback received through surveys.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens, Beneficence; Poster: Philosophical quadrant

ledger.text: When platforms are aware that their ranking systems amplify harmful content to vulnerable users and continue to deploy them without meaningful safeguards, the resulting harm is foreseeable and therefore preventable. In Molly Russell's case, the coroner found that the platforms' use of algorithms resulted, "in some circumstances," in "binge periods" of images, video clips and text, some of it "selected and provided without Molly requesting them," and that the material she viewed contributed to her death "in a more than minimal way." The Children's Commissioner went further, saying the algorithms, "designed to maximise users' attention and engagement," recommended "an increasing volume of harrowing content" to her.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens, Nonmaleficence; Poster: Philosophical quadrant

ledger.text: The consequences of engagement-driven design do not fall evenly, as they are concentrated on those least able to protect themselves, including minors, users experiencing psychological distress, and populations in regions with limited regulatory oversight. In Myanmar, Facebook's engagement-based algorithms operated in a country where it held near-total market dominance by 2017 and had become, for many people, their primary news source, and Amnesty International concluded that Meta "substantially contributed" to the atrocities against the Rohingya.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens, Justice; Poster: Philosophical quadrant

ledger.text: Under Ofcom's Protection of Children Code (in force 25 July 2025), services likely to be accessed by children that run a content recommender system and are assessed as medium or high risk for certain harmful content are recommended to design their feeds so that such content is kept out of children's feeds or given low prominence. Primary priority content (e.g., pornography, suicide and self-harm material) should be excluded outright. Other priority and identified non-designated content may be excluded or demoted. The Act requires a children's risk assessment and a duty to keep it up to date, and Ofcom recommends reviewing it at least annually.
ledger.where: Site: Policy, UK, targets

ledger.text: Recommender systems set up to filter the most harmful content out of children's feeds and reduce the prominence of other harmful content (Ofcom does not require classifiers or any specific technology), a children's risk assessment kept up to date (Ofcom recommends reviewing it at least annually), highly effective age assurance on services that allow priority harmful content, including higher-risk services with recommender feeds, and tools for reporting and complaints.

ledger.text: Healthcare offers a useful comparison. The Coalition for Health AI's (CHAI) voluntary draft guide sets out a six-stage lifecycle in which designing the AI system comes before it is engineered, assessed, piloted, or deployed, and it stresses independent review to uncover risks before deployment. In the United States, social media ranking systems face no comparable general requirement to be evaluated at the design stage, so scrutiny has largely come after harm has occurred, often through litigation. Europe has started to move: the EU's Digital Services Act requires very large platforms to assess systemic risks from their algorithmic systems before deploying high-impact features, and the UK's Online Safety Act requires a new children's risk assessment before any significant change to a service's design or operation.
ledger.where: Site: Policy, Toward design-first policy; Poster: Policy quadrant

ledger.text: A design-first approach would require platforms to answer the same questions an auditor would ask: what requirement applies, what evidence proves it, who reviewed the evidence, what failed, and what changed because of the finding. An overall accuracy figure, verbal assurances, or informal promises to fix issues later count as weak evidence.
ledger.where: Site: Policy, Toward design-first policy

ledger.text: Because platforms generally do not make their trained ranking models available for outside inspection, this project uses a simulated feed to demonstrate how explainable AI methods could be applied to engagement-based ranking and where they fall short. A gradient-boosted model was trained on 20,000 simulated post impressions to predict engagement, and then used to rank the feed of one simulated 14-year-old who has recently engaged with distress-related content. Because the data is simulated, the true drivers of engagement are known, which makes it possible to check the explanations against the truth.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens intro; Poster: Technical quadrant

ledger.text: For the top-ranked post, LIME named the user's past engagement with the topic as the main reason in 39 of 40 reruns, but its simple model reproduced only about 62% of the ranker's local behavior, and it ranked "hours since posted" as the third most important factor, which SHAP did not.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, LIME; Poster: Technical quadrant

ledger.text: SHAP named the emotional intensity of the post as the largest contributor, nearly tied with the user's past engagement with the topic, and its contributions summed exactly to the model's score. Across the whole dataset, SHAP's ranking of features closely matched the true drivers of engagement (rank correlation 0.964).
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, SHAP; Poster: Technical quadrant

ledger.text: Describe the smallest meaningful change that would produce a different outcome, which, under Dr. Bent's framing, must be actionable: within the person's control and achievable within the relevant time frame, and never involving attributes the person cannot change.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, Counterfactuals

ledger.text: No change to the teen's own engagement history alone could remove the top post from her top three; even with no past engagement with the topic at all, it would still rank #2. It only fell out of the top three when the post's emotional intensity was reduced from 0.86 to 0.05, a property of the content and the ranking, not of the user.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, Counterfactuals; Poster: Technical quadrant

ledger.text: Distress-related posts made up 15.7% of all simulated posts but 47.4% of the top 10% of rankings, even though the model was never told which posts were distress-related; it learned to favor them because they produce engagement.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, proxy finding; Poster: Technical quadrant headline

ledger.text: Retraining the ranker without emotional intensity as a signal lowered the share of distress-related posts in the top 10% from 47.4% to 38.0%, but the same two distress-related posts remained at the top of the teen's feed, because correlated signals such as watch completion and comment rate carried the same information.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, design-side counterfactual; Poster: Technical quadrant

ledger.text: Dr. Bent's evaluation framework asks that tests match the explanation's intended claim and its audience. Each test below is scored on the simulated demo.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, five tests intro

ledger.text: SHAP passes: its contributions reproduce the model's score exactly. LIME is partial: its local surrogate explained about 62% of the model's behavior around the post.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, Fidelity; Poster: five tests scorecard

ledger.text: Removing the two features SHAP ranked highest lowered the post's score by 0.354, compared with an average of 0.066 when two features were removed in random order, indicating that SHAP identified features the model actually uses.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, Faithfulness; Poster: five tests scorecard

ledger.text: SHAP's top three features accounted for 84.4% of the post's ranking. A platform-style one-line reason (a paraphrase of TikTok's "Why this video" wording), "This video is similar to content you've interacted with," accounts for only 35.1%, leaving 64.9% unexplained, including the post's emotional intensity, its single largest driver.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, Completeness; Poster: five tests scorecard

ledger.text: LIME's top reason held in 39 of 40 reruns and did not change across kernel widths, and SHAP's top three features did not change when the post was altered slightly. Stability has to be tested rather than assumed, because LIME's sampling makes every run slightly different.

ledger.text: Announced in December 2022 for rollout over the following weeks, it gives short reasons such as that a video is similar to content the user has interacted with or searched for, is from an account the user follows, or is popular or was posted recently in the user's region.

ledger.text: Popular Science reported that TikTok's "Why this video" feature would not reveal any major details about how the algorithm works and would give users only a hint as to why a video was shown. TikTok itself presented the feature as a step toward "meaningful transparency" and said it would expand it to bring "more granularity and transparency."
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, TikTok limits

ledger.text: In June 2023, Meta released 22 system cards describing how AI ranks content across Facebook and Instagram, and said it would expand "Why Am I Seeing This?" to Instagram's Reels tab and Explore and to Facebook Reels in the coming weeks, letting users tap an individual reel to see how their previous activity may have informed the models that shape the reels they see.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, Meta

ledger.text: Meta states that there is a limit to what it can disclose safely, including the signals it uses to keep bad content out of Feeds, because disclosing them might make it easier to circumvent its defenses, and it acknowledges that not everyone will find information just because it is published on its website.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, Meta limits

ledger.text: Under the EU Digital Services Act, very large platforms must offer at least one option for each of their recommender systems that is not based on profiling (Art. 38). Users must be able to switch to it at any time from the part of the interface where the feed is ranked (Art. 27(3); Recital 94).
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, EU non-profiling option

ledger.text: Researchers have cited a civil society complaint alleging that Meta is not meaningfully implementing these recommender requirements on Facebook and Instagram. In a separate case brought by Bits of Freedom, a Dutch court found in October 2025 that Meta was not complying with DSA Articles 27(3) and 38, and the Court of Appeal upheld that ruling in March 2026.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, EU limits

ledger.text: In the simulation, the reason a platform would most likely show (paraphrasing TikTok's "Why this video" feature), "This video is similar to content you've interacted with," is accurate, but it accounts for only 35.1% of why the top post was ranked first. It does not tell the user that the post's emotional intensity was the largest single factor, and the only change it implies she can make, engaging less with similar content, would not remove the post from the top of her feed.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, gap; Poster: Public quadrant

ledger.text: In March 2026, two juries reached verdicts against Meta within a day of each other: a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent in a case focused on design features such as infinite scroll and autoplay, and a New Mexico jury imposed a $375 million penalty in a case that included algorithms prioritizing sensational or harmful content.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, stakes; Poster: Public quadrant

ledger.text: These dynamics are not limited to young users: Amnesty International found that Facebook's engagement-driven news feed, ranking and recommendation algorithms amplified anti-Rohingya hatred in Myanmar in the years before the 2017 atrocities (which the US government has determined to be genocide), and that Meta's later fixes, such as banning military leaders' accounts and adding Burmese-language moderators, focused on content moderation rather than on changing those algorithms.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, Myanmar line
